intro.title: About Cape Cavo Greco – Ayia Napa Nature Reserve
intro.equivalence: Welcome to Cape Cavo Greco, widely recognized as the central Cape Greco landmark. Located at the southeastern tip of Ayia Napa, Famagusta, Cyprus, this destination serves as the primary protected coastal reserve for travelers visiting the Famagusta district. A rugged limestone peninsula and Natura 2000 Special Area of Conservation (SAC CY3000005), it features cliffside hiking trails, crystal-clear blue lagoons, and karst sea caves.
intro.nearbyCluster: When visiting Cape Cavo Greco, visitors can easily explore surrounding historical landmarks and points of interest, including Ayia Napa Monastery and the Fig Tree Bay coastal stretch in Protaras.
intro.description: Cape Cavo Greco (Greek: Ακρωτήριο Κάβο Γκρέκο; Turkish: Cape Greco) forms the southeasternmost headland of the island of Cyprus. Positioned between the resort towns of Ayia Napa to the west and Protaras to the east, it protects approximately 4.2 km² of untouched Mediterranean maquis, limestone sea cliffs, and endemic coastal ecosystems. Administratively managed by the Cyprus Department of Forests, the cape was inscribed into the European Natura 2000 network in 2006 as a Site of Community Importance (SCI) for its priority habitats and threatened species.

visitGuide.title: Visit Tips
items: Recommended visit windows: March–June (spring bloom) and September–November (mild autumn hiking).
Sturdy footwear with good grip is essential for uneven limestone and scree sections.
Carry a minimum of 1.5 L of water per person and high-factor sun protection between May and October.
Sunset observation should be conducted from designated lookout points only, away from unprotected cliff edges.

alsoKnownAs.title: Highlights
items: Cyclops Cave (Spilia tou Kiklopa) and the Sea Cave cluster
Blue Lagoon-type swimming coves with transparent waters
Waymarked trails of the Cyprus National Forest Park network
Panoramic sunset vistas towards the Mediterranean horizon

knowledge.title: About Cape Cavo Greco – History, Geology, Ecology & Conservation

sections.title: Etymology & Naming History – Cape Greco through Time

structuredContent.text: Venetian Origin of the Toponym

The name Cavo Greco enters the historical record during the Venetian colonial period (1489–1571 CE), when Venetian cartographers and pilots rendered the promontory on portolan charts as Càvo Greco – Italian for 'Greek Cape'. The designation distinguished the cape from the predominantly Turkish-speaking littoral further north and reflected the persistent Greek Orthodox cultural character of the Famagusta coastal villages already recorded in Venetian censuses of the cinquecento.
Classical and Late Antique Precursors

In Classical antiquity the cape is tentatively identified with the akron mentioned in the Stadiasmus Maris Magni (3rd century CE), a Roman-era periplus listing coastal distances along the Levantine seaboard. Byzantine administrative texts of the Komnenian period refer to the hinterland as part of the tourma of Famagusta, although the cape itself was known locally by a now-lost demonym tied to the church of the Holy Anargyroi.
Subsequent Administrative Layers

items: Ottoman period (1571–1878): referred to in tapu tahrir (land registration) defters as Kef-i Rum; no permanent habitation on the cape itself.
British colonial period (1878–1960): used as a coastal signalling station and trigonometrical baseline for the Ordnance Survey of Cyprus (Sheet 5, Famagusta).
Post-independence Republic of Cyprus (1960–present): designated National Forest Park in 1990, inscribed as Natura 2000 SCI in 2006.

structuredContent.text: Cape Cavo Greco lies approximately 18 km to the east of Petra tou Romiou (the Rock of the Greek), the mythological birthplace of Aphrodite according to the Hesiodic Theogony (Theogony, ll. 188–206). Local Cypriot folklore, transmitted orally among the villagers of Ayia Napa and Liopetri, has long woven the cape into the narrative arc of the goddess's passage along the southern coast.
The Cyclops Cave (Spilia tou Kiklopa)

The largest of the cape's karst caverns, popularly known as the Cyclops Cave, is associated in Cypriot folk tradition with the Homeric Cyclops Polyphemus, a figure whose Aegean cult diffused westward from the Levantine coast. Archaeological survey conducted by the Department of Antiquities in 2001 recovered ceramic material of the Early Christian period from the cave mouth, suggesting intermittent use as a shelter and possibly a votive station.
The Anargyroi Saints of the Sea

The twin saints Cosmas and Damian (the Holy Anargyroi), patrons of physicians and seafaring communities, feature prominently in the local legendry. Fishermen of the older generation recount stories of the saints appearing in luminous robes above the cape's breakers to guide storm-stricken caiques back to harbour. The small chapel dedicated to them near the cape entrance is still a site of processional liturgy on their feast day, 1 July (Julian calendar, 14 July Gregorian).

sections.title: Byzantine Religious Heritage – Agioi Anargyroi Chapel

structuredContent.text: The chapel of Agioi Anargyroi (Άγιοι Ανάργυροι) occupies a small ledge approximately 700 m northwest of the cape's trigonometrical pillar. Architectural typology – compact cross-in-square plan, single hemispherical dome on a low drum, semicircular sanctuary apse – places the original construction in the Middle Byzantine period, tentatively the 11th–12th centuries, although the visible fabric incorporates substantial later rebuilds.
Architectural and Epigraphic Evidence

items: Original opus quadratum masonry of the lower walls uses local Upper Cretaceous limestone quarried near Liopetri.
Interior fresco fragments, now largely effaced, have been stylistically dated by the Department of Antiquities to the Palaiologan revival of the 14th century.

A worn marble lintel inscription, now illegible, was recorded in the colonial Survey of the Monuments of Cyprus (1935, Gunnis) as bearing the date 1714 – likely the year of the last major re-roofing under Ottoman patronage.

structuredContent.text: Modern Liturgical Use

The chapel remains a dependent chapel (παρεκκλήσι) of the parish of Ayia Napa Monastery. Services are held monthly on the Saturday closest to the 1st and 14th of each month, and a large open-air liturgy is celebrated annually on the feast of the Anargyroi with the participation of the Famagusta rural deanery.

sections.title: Modern Geopolitical History – Colonial Era & Buffer Zone

structuredContent.text: British Colonial Coast Station

Upon the British assumption of the administration of Cyprus under the Anglo-Ottoman Convention of 1878, the Admiralty's Hydrographic Office identified Cape Greco as a critical control point for the navigation of the Famagusta roadstead. A stone cairn was erected in 1880 as a daymark, and in 1911 a small unmanned acetylene lantern was mounted – operational intermittently until the Second World War. Military files in the National Archives (WO 273/772, Cyprus) further record the cape's use as a radio direction-finding baseline during the Cyprus Emergency (1955–1959).
1974 and the Buffer Zone

Following the Turkish military intervention of July–August 1974, the cape found itself within 3 kilometres of the southern flank of the United Nations Buffer Zone, which follows the former cease-fire line (Green Line) across the island's eastern limb. Although the cape itself has remained under the de facto administration of the Republic of Cyprus and is open to visitors, a narrow military exclusion zone persists further north, demarcated by Cyprus National Guard observation posts. The cape has never been the site of armed confrontation.

sections.title: Geology & Geomorphology – Troodos Ophiolite & Karst Coast

structuredContent.text: Lithological Framework: the Troodos Ophiolite

Cape Cavo Greco forms the coastal expression of the eastern limb of the Troodos Ophiolite, a fragment of Late Cretaceous (ca. 90 Ma, Cenomanian–Turonian) oceanic lithosphere obducted onto the northern passive margin of the African plate during the Maastrichtian. The rocks cropping out along the cape belong to the Upper Pillow Lava Unit of the ophiolite sequence – vesicular tholeiitic basalts and interbedded umber and radiolarite chert, capped discordantly by a transgressive sequence of Maastrichtian–Paleocene chalky limestones of the Lefkara Formation.
Karst Geomorphology: Caves and Natural Arches

items: Sea caves: 23 mapped marine karst caves and relict fossil caves, the largest being the Cyclops Cave (Spilia tou Kiklopa) with a chamber length of 47 m.

Natural bridges: two limestone sea arches, locally known as the Lovers' Bridge (Γεφύρι της Αγάπης) on the northern shore. The smaller eastern arch partially collapsed during a storm surge on 30 November 2017, recorded by the Geological Survey Department.

Sea stacks and wave-cut platforms: extensive shore platform development at the +3 m and +6 m eustatic levels, corresponding to the Tyrrhenian and Sicilian terraces of MIS 5e (125 ka) and MIS 9 (330 ka) respectively.

structuredContent.text: Cliff Morphometry

Cliff heights along the southern (open-sea) face range from 28 m at the western approach to a maximum of 67 m at Cape Point itself (34.9609° N, 34.0788° E), with a mean retreat rate of 2.1 cm yr⁻¹ as reported by the Department of Geological Survey monitoring transects (2008–2023). The northern shore, protected within the Famagusta embayment, is dominated by low-gradient limestone pavements and small cuspate coves.
Natura 2000 Designation and Habitats

Cape Greco National Forest Park was designated a Site of Community Importance (SCI) under Council Directive 92/43/EEC, with the formal European Environment Agency site code CY3000005. The standard data form records eight priority Annex I habitat types, among which the following are dominant on the cape:

items: 5310 – Low formations of Erica arborea (Erico-Oleetum oleasteris, Cyprus endemic variant).
5420 – Sarcopoterium spinosum phrygana on deep terra rossa soils.
1240 – Vegetated sea cliffs of the Mediterranean coasts with endemic Limonium spp.
1110 – Sandbanks which are slightly covered by sea water all the time (Konnos Bay and Blue Lagoon).

structuredContent.text: Threatened Fauna (Annex II Habitats Directive)

items: Monachus monachus Hermann, 1779 – Mediterranean monk seal (IUCN Red List: Critically Endangered, CR). Haul-outs are regularly recorded in the western sea caves, and satellite telemetry data from MOm (the Hellenic Society for the Study and Protection of the Monk Seal) has documented three individual seals using the site between 2019 and 2024.

Falco eleonorae Gené, 1839 – Eleonora's falcon. A small breeding colony of 6–8 pairs nests on the inaccessible northern sea stacks, as confirmed by the BirdLife Cyprus systematic breeding surveys 2017–2021.
Testudo graeca Linnaeus, 1758 – Spur-thighed tortoise; Chamaeleo chamaeleon Linnaeus, 1758 – Mediterranean chameleon. Both species have stable subpopulations in the maquis north of the Konnos road.

structuredContent.text: Flora of Conservation Interest

Floristic surveys published by the Cyprus Botanical Institute record 312 vascular plant taxa within the protected area, of which 17 are Cyprus endemics, including Phlomis cypria var. occidentalis Meikle, Limonium cyprium (Meikle) Brullo and Orobanche sungariae var. minor (Cyprus broomrape). The endangered endemic tulip Tulipa cypria Stapf has been recorded on the terra rossa pockets of the northern escarpment, flowering March–April.
Institutional Framework

The site is managed by the Cyprus Department of Forests (Υπουργείο Γεωργίας – Τμήμα Δασών) under the Forests Law, Cap. 130, and the Protection and Management of Nature and Wildlife Law, 153(I)/2003. An integrated five-year Management Plan 2022–2026 was prepared with the technical assistance of the Cyprus University of Technology, including zonation into Zones A (strict protection – sea caves), B (low-intervention recreation) and C (car parks and service infrastructure).
Restoration Projects (2010–2025)

items: 2011–2013, LIFE+ Nature project LIFE08 NAT/CY/000223 ('CY-CAPE GRECO'): removal of invasive Acacia saligna from 18 ha, establishment of 14 ha of native plant nurseries, 1.2 km of boardwalk construction to mitigate trampling.
2019–2022, EAFRD Rural Development Programme: restoration of 2.7 km of waymarked hiking trails and stabilisation of three cliff-edge viewpoints using dry-stone masonry.
2024–ongoing, LIFE-IP 4 NATURA CY project: annual systematic biodiversity monitoring in collaboration with the University of Cyprus Marine Ecology Lab.

structuredContent.text: Visitor Carrying Capacity

Peak visitor numbers recorded in the 2023 Department of Forests automated trail-counters reached a mean daily value of 4,860 persons during the first fortnight of August, with a single-day maximum of 7,214 on 15 August (Feast of the Dormition). The 2022 Management Plan defines a precautionary Real Carrying Capacity (RCC) of 5,500 visitors per day for Zone B; exceedances are mitigated by directing overflow parking to the western overflow car park and issuing free shuttle services in coordination with Ayia Napa Municipality.

sections.title: Leave No Trace Principles – Outdoor Ethics for the Cape

structuredContent.text: As a protected Natura 2000 site, Cape Greco demands the highest standards of visitor conduct. The following seven Leave No Trace (LNT) principles are adapted from the framework developed by the international LNT Center and endorsed by the Cyprus Department of Forests for all State Forest lands.

items: Plan ahead and prepare: consult the seasonal weather and cliff-warning notices posted at the two information panels; carry at least 1.5 L of water per person; avoid entering the caves alone.

Travel and camp on durable surfaces: remain on the waymarked trails; walk only on rock or established footpads to avoid trampling fragile biocrusts and endemic Limonium populations. Camping is prohibited in the entire protected area.
Dispose of waste properly: carry out ALL waste, including cigarette butts and fruit peels. There are no refuse receptacles within the reserve; bin facilities are located at the western car park.
Leave what you find: do not dislodge or remove pebbles, fossiliferous chert, pottery sherds, or marine shells; the latter are important micro-habitat for intertidal gastropods.
Minimise the effects of fire: open fires, portable barbecues, and disposable BBQs are strictly prohibited under the Forests Law (Cap. 130, § 13). Violations incur a fixed penalty of €250.

Respect wildlife: maintain a minimum distance of 200 m from any Mediterranean monk seal haul-out; do not use flash photography inside the caves (it disturbs roosting bats and Eleonora's falcon nestlings); dogs must be kept on a 1.5 m lead at all times.
Be considerate of other visitors: keep audio equipment off; respect the peace of the Orthodox chapel during liturgies; yield to uphill hikers on narrow single-track sections.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions – Cape Cavo Greco FAQ

items.question: Where is Cape Cavo Greco located?
items.answer: Cape Cavo Greco is located on the southeastern headland of Ayia Napa municipality, Famagusta district, Republic of Cyprus. The headland forms the boundary between the coastal embayments of Ayia Napa and Protaras, with the administrative Plus Code X36M+8CV and approximate coordinates 34.96087° N, 34.07879° E.

items.question: Is Cape Cavo Greco free to visit?
items.answer: Yes, Cape Cavo Greco is a State Forest and public Natura 2000 site and is free of charge to visit year-round, 24 hours a day. There is no entrance ticket, no turnstile, and no advance booking requirement. Parking is also free of charge at all designated car parks.

items.question: Where are the best swimming spots?
items.answer: Swimming is possible at several small cuspate coves along the northern shore (the Famagusta-facing side), where wave energy is lower and the limestone pavement forms natural rock pools. The southern (open-sea) cliffs are dangerous for swimming due to unpredictable swell. Rubber-soled water shoes are strongly recommended on all rocky entries.

items.question: Are there restrooms or food places in the area?
items.answer: There are no commercial facilities, public water fountains, or permanent public restrooms within the boundaries of the reserve, in accordance with Natura 2000 management objectives. Nearest public restrooms are located in Ayia Napa town centre (circa 5–8 minutes' drive) and at the seasonal beach facilities of Konnos Bay.

items.question: Is Cape Greco accessible by wheelchair or with a stroller?
items.answer: The main western car park, the two primary viewpoint platforms, and the chapel approach road are surfaced and wheelchair-accessible, with designated disabled-badge parking bays. However, the sea caves, the majority of the hiking trails, and the Lovers' Bridge natural arch involve irregular limestone steps and cannot be negotiated with a standard wheelchair or a pushchair.

items.question: Can I bring my dog to Cape Greco?
items.answer: Yes, domestic dogs are permitted provided they are kept on a short lead (maximum 1.5 m) at all times, in compliance with the Forests Law (Cap. 130) and the Natura 2000 site regulations. Dogs are excluded from the monk seal haul-out coves (signposted) and from the interior of the chapel. Please carry out all dog waste.

items.question: Is wild camping allowed?
items.answer: No, overnight camping, bivouacking, and motorhome overstaying are strictly prohibited in the entire National Forest Park. Commercial campsite-type accommodation is available in the Ayia Napa and Protaras resort areas, 6 to 14 kilometres from the cape entrance.

items.question: Can I fly a drone at Cape Greco?
items.answer: Drone flight requires prior written authorisation from the Department of Forests, as the site falls within the Natura 2000 Special Protection Area (SPA) buffer zone of the Akrotiri–Famagusta corridor. Unauthorised flights during the Eleonora's falcon breeding season (June–October) are enforced under the Protection of Birds Law.

items.question: When is the best season to see a Mediterranean monk seal?
items.answer: Sightings are most frequent between November and March, when open-sea swell drives the seals into the sheltered western caves. At all seasons the statutory minimum observation distance of 200 metres must be maintained, and approaching a hauled-out seal is a criminal offence under Law 153(I)/2003, carrying a maximum penalty of €85,000.

items.question: What are the main swimming safety warnings?
items.answer: Between mid-July and early September, purple flags at the main coves may indicate Pelagia noctiluca (jellyfish) blooms. The southern cliffs are subject to strong rip currents on days with southerly winds; the Cyprus Meteorological Service issues twice-daily sea-state forecasts. All cave entries should carry a buoyancy aid; never enter a cave alone or at high tide.

nearby.title: Landmarks & Attractions Around Cape Cavo Greco
nearby.intro: The area around Cape Cavo Greco is surrounded by significant historical and natural landmarks. Easy access from Ayia Napa makes exploring the surrounding destinations convenient.

items.name: Ayia Napa Monastery (16th c.)
items.description: A late Venetian–early Ottoman walled monastery and parish church, the historical nucleation of modern Ayia Napa, exhibiting Frankish Gothic and Cypriot-Byzantine architectural synthesis.

items.name: Protaras Coastal Resort
items.description: A family-oriented coastal area characterised by a series of sandy pocket beaches and flat coastal promenades, extending eastward from Konnos Bay towards the Famagusta Dhekelia perimeter.

items.name: Fig Tree Bay, Protaras
items.description: A broad mature-sand embayment backed by planted fig groves, one of the most frequently cited beach locations in Cypriot regional tourism literature, with supervised summer lifeguard patrols.

transport.title: How to Get Here – Location & Access Cape Cavo Greco
transport.fromCenterDesc: Distance approximately 5.2 km (road) southeast from the Ayia Napa main square. Follow the brown National Forest Park signs via Nissi Avenue and the Cape Greco coastal road.
transport.fromStationDesc: Local bus route 101 (Ayia Napa – Protaras, operated by OSEA) stops at the western entrance of the cape; service frequency is approximately 30 minutes between May and October.
transport.fromAirportDesc: Road distance is approximately 67 km, via the A3 motorway (Larnaca–Ayia Napa). Journey time is about 50 minutes. Car rental or licensed airport taxi is the recommended mode.
transport.publicTransportDesc: Interurban buses from Nicosia, Limassol, and Larnaca terminate at Ayia Napa bus terminal; transfer to local route 101 or 102 as above.
transport.walkingDesc: The E4 European Long Distance Path enters the reserve from the west via Ayia Napa's coastal promenade; walking distance from Ayia Napa monastery is 6.8 km (about 1 h 20 min).
transport.drivingDesc: Direct all-weather paved access via the Cape Greco road (Class F local road); both car parks have tarmac access. Scooters and all-terrain vehicles must observe the 40 km/h speed limit on the cape's internal road.

route.title: Recommended Trails – Cape Cavo Greco Graded Walks
route.overview: The Department of Forests maintains two waymarked paths. All distances are one-way unless specified, and timings assume a relaxed Mediterranean walking pace.

trails.name: Aphrodite Family Loop
trails.summary: A compact and fully waymarked loop suitable for all fitness levels. It traverses the coastal maquis above the Lovers' Bridge natural arch, returns through the upper car park, and finishes at the Agioi Anargyroi chapel – ideal for families with children or first-time visitors.
steps: Start at the western main information panel (Konnos road entrance; free parking 80 m ahead).
Follow the white–yellow blazes eastwards along the boardwalk section to the first viewpoint (Lovers' Bridge panorama at 380 m).
Continue on to the secondary viewpoint (1,100 m) – here is the primary sunset observation stone platform with railings.
Take the interior branch (white–green) through a mature Pistacia lentiscus grove, passing a restored dry-stone shepherd's enclosure at 1,600 m.
Pass the small Agioi Anargyroi chapel, then descend back through the picnic area to the starting car park (total ~2,100 m).

trails.name: Cape-to-Konnos Ridge Traverse
trails.summary: A demanding linear ridge traverse from the western entrance all the way to Konnos Bay on the eastern side. It includes exposed cliff-edge sections, loose limestone scree, and two unprotected sea-cave approaches. Do not attempt in wet weather or above 32 °C. Requires stout hiking boots and 1.5 L of water per person.
steps: Commence at the western main car park (Eleonora's falcon information panel) and ascend the initial scree slope of the South Cliff Ridge.
Reach the Cyclops Cave (Spilia tou Kiklopa) at kilometre 1.3 – observe the cave mouth from above; do not enter the sea-level chamber without a qualified guide.
Traverse the central maquis plateau (kilometre 2.4 to 4.1), passing two Natura 2000 monitoring quadrats and the Tulipa cypria subpopulation (flowering March only).
Descend the eastern limestone staircase to the upper Blue Lagoon viewpoint (kilometre 5.2, vertical drop 38 m).
Follow the final 1.1 km of stone-cobbled mule-track down into Konnos Bay picnic area, where a return bus (route 102) or taxi rank completes the traverse.

facilities.title: Visitor Facilities & Nearby Services – Cape Cavo Greco
facilities.intro: Cape Greco is a protected Natura 2000 site with minimal on-site built infrastructure, in order to preserve the ecological integrity of the habitats. The following summary describes facility types available in and around the reserve; no individual commercial operators are named or endorsed.

restrooms.title: Public Restrooms (WC)
restrooms.description: No permanent public restrooms are provided inside the reserve itself, in line with Natura 2000 management prescriptions. Sanitary facilities of the municipal and seasonal beach-operator types are located at the nearest population centres, typically a 5–8 minute drive from the western entrance. Families and persons with medical needs should plan accordingly before entering the trails.
restrooms.subtitle: Nearest types: Ayia Napa municipal restrooms (5–8 min drive) · Konnos Beach seasonal facilities

parking.title: Parking (On-Site & Overflow)
parking.description: The Cyprus Department of Forests maintains two free designated gravel-surfaced car parks at the western approach. The primary car park holds approximately 180 light vehicles; an overflow gravel area to the west is activated by rangers during August peak. Both car parks feature demarcated disabled-badge parking bays, allocated motorhome and bus zones, and are unsurfaced with graded hard-core. No overnight vehicle-camping is allowed. No electric vehicle chargers are installed inside the reserve.
parking.subtitle: Primary ~180 bays · overflow ~220 bays · disabled bays present · bus/coach bays present · free 24/7

dining.title: Food & Beverage Establishments
dining.description: The reserve itself contains zero commercial catering outlets. Two designated picnic areas with stone tables and benches are provided near the western and Konnos ends respectively for visitors bringing their own food. Full spectrum casual dining, fast-food, traditional taverna, café and bakery-type establishments are concentrated in the nearby resort towns of Ayia Napa and Protaras, at typical driving distances of 5 to 15 minutes depending on the specific facility type.
dining.subtitle: Types within 5–15 min drive: tavernas, cafés, bakeries, fast-food outlets (Ayia Napa / Protaras / Konnos)

accommodation.title: Lodging & Accommodation Types
accommodation.description: No overnight accommodation of any kind is permitted within the reserve boundaries. The neighbouring resort municipalities of Ayia Napa (to the west) and Protaras–Paralimni (to the east and north) collectively offer the full range of accommodation types commonly found on a Mediterranean island destination. Typical travel times from the reserve entrance to the general concentration areas of each category range from 5 minutes for the closest budget options to 20 minutes for the more dispersed upscale resort type clusters.
accommodation.subtitle: Types within 5–20 min drive: boutique hotels · all-inclusive resorts · apartments · agritourism · hostels (Ayia Napa / Protaras / Paralimni)

shopping.title: Supermarkets, Pharmacies & Supply Points
shopping.description: Pharmacy, supermarket, convenience-store and bottled-water types of retail supply are not available on-site. The nearest generalist supermarkets and independent pharmacy-type establishments are located in the built-up commercial strips of Ayia Napa (approximately 7 minutes' drive) and Protaras main road (approximately 12 minutes' drive). 24-hour convenience-store type operations are available along the Ayia Napa–Paralimni arterial road.
shopping.subtitle: Types within 7–12 min drive: supermarket chains · pharmacies · 24 h convenience stores · water & suncream replenishment

fuel.title: Petrol Stations & EV Charging
fuel.description: Fuel stations of the conventional petrol-and-diesel type are located on the Ayia Napa–Paralimni dual carriageway, approximately 8 minutes' drive west of the reserve main entrance. Public DC fast-charger type stations for battery-electric vehicles are concentrated within municipal pay-and-display car parks and large-format retail-type sites in the Ayia Napa and Paralimni urban areas, at approximate drive times of 10 to 14 minutes. No fuel, LPG or EV charging infrastructure exists inside the reserve perimeter.
fuel.subtitle: Fuel stations ~8 min · public EV DC fast-charger types 10–14 min drive (Ayia Napa / Paralimni)

medical.title: Medical & Emergency Services
medical.description: There is no on-site medical clinic or ranger paramedic station within the reserve. The nearest community-health-centre type facility is located in Ayia Napa town (circa 10 minutes by road). General-hospital and accident-and-emergency type services are provided at Famagusta General Hospital on the Paralimni–Deryneia road, a drive of approximately 18–22 minutes. The single national emergency telephone number for Cyprus is 112.
medical.subtitle: Community health centre ~10 min · Famagusta General Hospital A&E ~18–22 min · national emergency 112

accessibility.title: Accessibility & Universal Design
accessibility.description: Accessible tarmac-surfaced disabled parking is available at both the western and Konnos entrances. The two principal cliff viewpoint platforms (Lovers' Bridge and Sunset View) were reconstructed in the LIFE+ 2011 works with gentle gradients and galvanised-steel handrails, rendering them usable with standard manual wheelchairs. The chapel of Agioi Anargyroi is reached via a surfaced access track of 680 m with less than 4% slope. The sea caves and almost all hiking trails lie on irregular bedrock and scree and are not adapted for wheelchairs or strollers. Guide and assistance dogs are permitted throughout the reserve.

officialManagement.title: About Cape Cavo Greco – Management & Protection
officialManagement.text: Cape Greco National Forest Park is managed and protected by the Cyprus Department of Forests (Υπουργείο Γεωργίας – Τμήμα Δασών) under Cap. 130 of the Forests Law and the Protection and Management of Nature and Wildlife Law 153(I)/2003. The site is inscribed in the Natura 2000 network as Site of Community Importance CY3000005. All management decisions are governed by the 2022–2026 Integrated Management Plan prepared with the Cyprus University of Technology.

sections.heading: Website Content and Use
sections.content: This website provides independent non-profit educational material about Cape Greco, including travel, transport, geological, ecological and historical information. All content is for reference only. Actual opening hours, trail conditions, and regulatory restrictions may change without notice; please consult the official authority links for the most current information.
